headline: University of Oxford physicists have linked separate trapped-ion modules built from two different kinds of atom and kept the shared quantum link alive in memory for more than 10 seconds.
score_reason: Pool score kept: a peer-reviewed laboratory advance in quantum networking, but small in scale and reported through one trade site's summary.
importance_line: Researchers building networks of linked quantum computers and quantum sensors gain a way to hold a link between separate machines long enough to use it, but this is a laboratory demonstration with up to four qubits and the details come from one trade outlet's summary of the paper.
summary: Quantum Computing Report reports that University of Oxford physicists, in a paper in Physical Review Letters, linked separate trapped-ion modules (devices that hold charged atoms as quantum bits) by using strontium ions to exchange light and calcium ions to store the result, creating entanglement (a quantum link between particles) among up to four qubits and keeping it for more than 10 seconds. That is more than 100 times longer than the roughly 100 milliseconds it took to create, which the report says removes a major obstacle to distributed quantum computing and quantum sensing networks.
notes: The publication date of the paper is not stated, so it is treated as new on the date of the trade report (17 Oct 2026). The paper was not opened.
